title: You’ve probably heard it and felt the tension immediately.
paragraphs: You’ve probably heard it and felt the tension immediately.
How could a holy God command entire groups—giants, whole bloodlines—to be wiped out?
It doesn’t sit comfortably. It shouldn’t.
Because if you rush past it, you miss what was really happening beneath the surface… and what it reveals about God, sin, and the war most people don’t even realize they’re in.

They read about the Nephilim in Genesis, the Anakim in Canaan, the towering figures that made Israel say, “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes” (Numbers 13:33)… and they reduce it to myth, exaggeration, or primitive warfare.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The Bible never presents this as a normal conflict.
“The Nephilim were on the earth in those days… when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them.”
Something crossed a boundary God had established.
Something corrupted what was meant to be purely human.
You’ve been told God is love.
But you were never told what His love is willing to confront.
Because love that refuses to confront corruption… isn’t love. It’s surrender.
Scripture repeatedly shows they were tied to deep rebellion against God—spiritual and physical.
By the time Israel enters Canaan, these groups—the Anakim, Rephaim, and others—are not just large in stature, but entrenched in violent, idolatrous systems that defied God completely.
“It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord your God is driving them out before you.”
And judgment always has a reason.
But then the question gets sharper.
Why not just remove them or reform them?

The biblical narrative points to something deeply corrupted—something beyond moral failure. A line that had become so intertwined with rebellion against God that preserving it would mean preserving the corruption itself.
You don’t negotiate with a cancer that’s spreading through the body.
He is patient… but not passive.
And then it gets even closer.
Because you start to see a pattern.

Genesis 6 — corruption spreads → God judges with the flood
Canaan — corruption spreads → God judges through Israel
The cross — sin spreads → God judges… but this time…
Because the same God who judged the giants…
Stepped into humanity to save sinners.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
But you were born in sin.
“You were dead in the trespasses and sins…”
He made a way for your redemption.
But that doesn’t mean He ignores sin now.
It means He placed your judgment on Christ—if you receive Him.
A window you’re still inside right now.
That moment when you knew something in your life wasn’t right.
Told yourself it wasn’t that serious.
Because truth doesn’t disappear just because it’s uncomfortable.
The same God who judged corruption in the past…
The difference is—you’re being offered grace first.
“The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.”
Because this isn’t a casual invitation.
It’s a rescue before judgment comes.
Two futures are in front of you.
One where you keep delaying, keep rationalizing, keep living on your terms…
And one where you finally surrender.
If something in you is tightening right now…
Say it plainly, even if it costs your pride:
Because silence has kept you stuck long enough.
If this opened your eyes even a little, don’t keep it to yourself.
Someone else is asking the same question—but they’re too afraid to say it.
You know who came to mind.
Because conviction fades when it’s ignored.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—not just informed, but transformed—step into that next level of discipleship here:
For growth that actually leads somewhere.
Because the God who judged the giants…
Is the same God offering you grace.
But that window won’t stay open forever.
